reason: Hip-fracture PT began at moderate-to-maximal assist with weakness; this need is skilled rehabilitation, and moving from dependence is not maintenance-level, so the necessity objection is unsupported.
The submitted 12-day hospital stay exceeds 3 days, and the record shows repeated medication adjustments for fluctuating blood pressure and heart rate by nursing, supporting skilled need.
The facts only recite the appellant's notice arguments; no clinical facts show an inpatient level of care was needed, and the QIO notice says routine short-stay cases would be denied.
The facts are procedural only and show no qualifying hospital stay or skilled care, so coverage is not supported.

Admission followed a qualifying hospital stay, but PT was discharged on Feb 7 for plateau and a non-coverage notice was issued around Feb 15, so the early stay is supported and the later period is not.
Nothing in the facts shows the assisted living residence qualifies as home, homebound status, or a certification, so coverage is not supported.
Skilled PT and OT ended in January 2009, before the disputed dates beginning January 28, and no skilled services are shown on those dates.

Nurses repeatedly assessed and monitored, and arranged physician-directed insulin changes, medication non-compliance problems and a UTI in a legally blind diabetic, which is documented skilled observation.
The Feb 12-17 stay counts as at least 3 inpatient days (admission day counted), SNF admission was direct, and a physician ordered skilled nursing to monitor hematuria and the catheter.

Qualifying stay and direct admission support coverage while skilled PT/OT continued, but therapy ended Sept 30 for medical reasons and the facts do not support continued rehabilitative coverage afterward.
Skilled PT with steady progress after the Sept 2 fall supports coverage, but the appellant concedes goals were met by Sept 11, 2008, so later services are not shown necessary.
Stair-lift and stair-safety PT instruction is reasonable and necessary, but visits solely to train aides or set up an aide program are not billable.
The beneficiary had recurrent UTIs, urosepsis, bleeding, abscesses and a fistula, so nursing evaluation of complications is skilled and documented, distinct from routine ostomy care.
Part-time or intermittent home health is covered only up to the limits (under 8 hours daily and 28 hours weekly), so hours up to the limit may be covered and hours beyond are not.
Placement in a noncertified bed is payable only under limitation-of-liability conditions, and the facts do not show those conditions were met.
The facts are procedural only and contain no beneficiary-level assessments showing IRF coverage criteria were met.
A qualifying stay and skilled nursing and PT support coverage in early August through behavior stabilization and pneumonia treatment, but the facts do not support skilled need through August 31.
Post-knee-replacement IRF stay with IV/IM medication, severe pain managed by PCA, and moderate-to-maximal assistance needs after prior independence shows reasonable and necessary IRF care.
